extracted.intended_audience: Authors of systematic reviews in public health; evidence synthesis methodologists and guideline developers
extracted.subtask_short: writing systematic reviews for public health
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, conducting and reporting systematic reviews of public health interventions, addressing question framing, equity, intervention complexity, risk-of-bias appraisal across diverse study designs, and synthesis methods when meta-analysis is not possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and meaningful review objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: To be useful, systematic reviews must address clear and meaningful objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the objectives carefully (where possible involving stakeholder perspectives) so the review addresses important questions for decision makers. Planning objectives early helps design analyses that reflect review aims and user needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for complexity and avoid post-hoc selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning at an early stage can minimize bias arising from post hoc selection while improving clarity for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate variations in interventions, populations and contexts; pre-specify grouping and analysis plans to reduce post-hoc decisions that can bias findings. Use logic models and conceptual frameworks to map concepts and likely effect modifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use logic models and conceptual frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic models and conceptual frameworks may help to think through the important concepts within the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these tools during planning to identify mechanisms, components, populations, outcomes and contextual factors that matter to the review question and subsequent syntheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define eligibility criteria and review scope clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: The eligibility criteria of the review should clearly define the review’s scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured approaches (for example PICO: population, intervention, comparator, outcome) to define inclusion criteria. Provide enough detail that study selection for a particular group or synthesis could be replicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify how groups will be used in syntheses (transparent grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should specify how groups (population or intervention groups) will be used in specific syntheses or comparisons, in enough detail that the selection of studies for inclusion in a group or synthesis could be replicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present clear definitions of each group and a rationale for grouping choices. Example: a school-based physical activity review presented an overall synthesis followed by analyses by defined intervention types (enhanced PE, other school-time activity, before/after school, multi-component).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider equity throughout the review
rubrics_metrics.description: Considering equity explicitly in systematic reviews from question formulation to interpretation adds value to the review’s findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address equity at each stage—formulation, data collection, analysis and interpretation—so end users can understand how findings apply to diverse populations and whether aggregated results obscure important differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PROGRESS-Plus to identify relevant equity factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider possible differences across PROGRESS-Plus factors (place, race/ethnicity/culture/language, occupation, gender/sex, religion, education, socioeconomic status, social capital, plus age, sexual orientation, disability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and focus on those PROGRESS-Plus elements most relevant to the review question; use them to plan subgroup analyses, data extraction and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe included populations and differential inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the included populations using relevant PROGRESS-Plus elements, and record whether participants with particular characteristics are less likely to be included or more likely to withdraw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and report data on population characteristics and differential recruitment/attrition so reviewers can assess applicability and equity implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and report outcomes important to different populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure different outcomes that are of importance to different populations (e.g. developmental outcomes for children, measures of social participation for older adults).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan to include and report outcomes that matter for specific groups identified by equity considerations, not only aggregated clinical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate population/setting differences in summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Key differences in populations or settings should be clearly communicated in summary versions of the review (such as ‘Summary of findings’ tables and abstracts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present stratified findings (for example by low- vs high-mortality settings) when context meaningfully modifies expected outcomes; ensure summaries highlight applicability and limitations across settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and address intervention complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Public health interventions are often multi-component and may involve interactions between components, participants and context; sometimes a systems perspective is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether exhaustive listing of components adds value. Think about interactions, long causal pathways, implementation variability and whether a systems perspective (intervention as event in adaptive system) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify common elements and theorized modes of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the common elements of an intervention that are hypothesized to bring about the desired effects (components, theoretical approaches or modes of action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus analyses on elements likely driving effect rather than on every component; use taxonomies or intervention classifications where useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose analysis methods suited to complexity (including qualitative/process evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most useful review may not estimate a universal effect but explore why/how an intervention succeeded in specific cases, necessitating different analysis approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider qualitative syntheses of feasibility/acceptability, process and implementation outcomes, or exploration of factors associated with successful outcomes when complexity or context is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select study designs appropriate to the review question
rubrics_metrics.description: The study designs included in any systematic review should be those appropriate to answer the review question (randomized trials may not always be feasible or ethical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify inclusion of randomized and/or non-randomized designs according to the question and consider implications for bias and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider bias and conflicts of interest in included studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Use evidence-based methods to identify risk factors associated with bias in results and discuss the role of conflict of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly assess and report potential biases and conflicts across included studies; consider their impact on syntheses and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess risk of bias due to missing results
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess risks of bias arising from missing results (e.g. unpublished studies or unreported outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Chapter 13 guidance on missing results; consider how missing evidence could distort the synthesis and whether sensitivity analyses or downgrading certainty are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate risk-of-bias tools (RoB 2 and ROBINS-I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply RoB 2 for randomized trials (including cluster trials) and ROBINS-I for non-randomized studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both tools provide structured signalling questions; use available templates and resources (e.g. https://riskofbias.info and available Excel tools) and consult examples in the Cochrane Library.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternative synthesis methods when meta-analysis is not possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When studies lack necessary data for meta-analysis, use alternative statistical synthesis methods such as summary statistics to describe ranges, vote counting based on direction of effect, or combining P values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 12 describes methods and companion visual displays (box plots, harvest plots, albatross plots). These approaches can structure analysis when effect estimates with variances are unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visual displays and structured presentation for non-meta-analytic syntheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Companion visual displays for alternative synthesis methods include box plots, harvest plots and albatross plots; structured tabulation or plotting may be used when synthesis is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual and tabular presentation helps make sense of many studies or complex interventions and avoids unwieldy text descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid synthesis when inappropriate and present results transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: Synthesis may be inappropriate where included studies are at high risk of bias or there are concerns about missing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases, present structured tabulation or plotting without combining results; be explicit about reasons for not synthesizing and limitations for decision making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-specify and report synthesis methods using reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the use of alternative synthesis methods at the protocol stage and report them completely in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use updated PRISMA 2020 and the SWiM (Synthesis Without Meta-analysis) reporting guideline to guide specification and transparent reporting of synthesis methods.
